speakers.name: Dr. Maya Chen
speakers.background: Dr. Chen is a cognitive neuroscientist with 11 years of experience developing and evaluating EEG-based attention measures in children and adolescents. She has led signal-processing work on dry-electrode systems, including artifact rejection, spectral-feature extraction, and within-child change analyses in noisy real-world settings. Her prior studies have mostly been conducted in supervised research sessions rather than full classrooms.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Maya treats the pilot as a test of whether a neurophysiological signal can be measured reliably enough in a classroom to support a meaningful brain–behavior analysis. She is focused on session-level EEG signal quality, movement and contact artifacts, the validity of the attention marker, and whether changes in that marker covary with independently collected attendance and learning-related outcomes. She distinguishes feasibility of recording from evidence that neurofeedback affects educational outcomes.

speakers.name: Elena Ruiz

Her work examines how classroom interventions fit daily routines, how implementation burdens fall on teachers, and how administrative data and school assessments can be used without disrupting instruction. speakers.distinct_perspective: Elena evaluates the program through the realities of a Grade 4 classroom: protected instructional time, teacher workload, student comfort, and whether participation is distributed fairly rather than limited to students who are easiest to schedule or manage. speakers.name: Arun Patel
speakers.background: Arun Patel is a biomedical engineer with 13 years of experience building wearable physiological-sensing systems for pediatric and consumer health research. transcript.speaker: Elena Ruiz
transcript.text: Good morning, everyone. Before we get into the details, I want to make sure we leave today with a school-facing plan that's actually manageable. The eight-week schedule, the consent materials, and a clear answer on what staff have to do when the device doesn't behave as expected. The independent-work block is still the best fit, but the clock time- it moves around more than the written schedule suggests.

transcript.speaker: Arun Patel
transcript.text: Mm, right.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Sorry, I’m a couple minutes late—where have we got to? Elena, on that moving block time, do the activities themselves vary too across rooms? I’m thinking, for the EEG, the clock matters less than the actual activity. Quiet individual reading versus small-group rotation will give us pretty different low-frequency movement contamination.

transcript.speaker: Elena Ruiz
transcript.text: They do vary. Most teachers described it as individual reading or written work, but on pullout days it can turn into catch-up work, and sometimes there are quieter rotations. I don't think we can promise one uniform activity across all four rooms, so what's the minimum we need teachers to note without creating a second set of paperwork, because—

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Keep it really light, I think. Just one activity code, individual reading, written work, rotation, or catch-up, and then a note only if there was an obvious disruption or the child left their seat. The device stream gives us contact and gross artifact metrics, but without that context I can't tell whether elevated delta is physiology or just a room doing something different.

transcript.speaker: Elena Ruiz
transcript.text: One code and an exception note is probably the outer limit. But I wouldn't have the classroom teacher enter it after the fact. If the aide is there for the sessions, they can do a quick session check on the study tablet. Maya, if we only have that context for some sessions because staffing shifts, does that make the analysis unusable, or is partial coverage enough?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Partial coverage is still usable, as long as we capture when there isn't a code, so it doesn't look like a normal session. I'd use the activity field as an adjustment variable and do a sensitivity analysis on the coded subset. It just means we shouldn't infer too much from a delta shift in an uncoded session. The contact and artifact stream still has to be complete for every recording.

transcript.speaker: Elena Ruiz
transcript.text: Okay, that distinction helps.

transcript.speaker: Arun Patel
transcript.text: We can capture the missing activity code explicitly on the tablet, so it won’t get silently treated as a normal entry. On the contact and artifact stream, though, I want to check with Maya. After rejection, how much clean within-session data do you, you need before you’d call that recording analytically useful?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: I’d want at least eight clean minutes, preferably spread across the block rather than just one clean patch at the start. But I don’t want to lock the exclusion threshold from the usability study yet. The low-frequency contamination we’re seeing in these nominally good-contact sessions could make that cutoff too, too optimistic. Arun, did your low-contact sessions tend to fail early, or was it more about fit and head size?

transcript.speaker: Arun Patel
transcript.text: In the usability sessions, it was mostly fit, not a simple early failure. A few children had acceptable contact at startup, then it drifted once they settled into work or moved, and that happened more often at the smaller head sizes. I’d be a little careful about calling those nominally good-contact sessions good until I check whether the firmware flag is averaging over too long a window.

transcript.speaker: Elena Ruiz
transcript.text: That is exactly the piece I need translated into a staff response. If contact drifts, does the aide just see a simple prompt to reseat the band and continue, or are they expected to judge whether the session has failed? With two 12-minute sessions a week across four Grade 4 classrooms, we cannot make them, them into data monitors.

transcript.speaker: Arun Patel
transcript.text: They shouldn't have to judge it. The tablet can give a simple reseat prompt after a sustained contact drop, and the aide just tries once. Then they mark “unable to restore” if it keeps going, and the headband still keeps the timestamp and quality record. Elena, is there actually someone in each room during independent work who can do that without pulling the teacher away—

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Hm, that's the constraint.

transcript.speaker: Elena Ruiz
transcript.text: In three of the four rooms, I think we can arrange for an aide or the study staff member to be there for the session. I wouldn't assume the classroom teacher can step away. The fourth is less certain, and I don't want enrollment there to depend on which children need the least support. Could the reseat prompt, um, wait for the study aide when one isn't immediately available, instead of asking the teacher to intervene?

transcript.speaker: Arun Patel
transcript.text: It can wait. We can make the prompt non-blocking. It logs the contact drop and keeps recording, and the aide can reseat it when they arrive. Nobody has to decide whether to end the session. I’d want the tablet to show it’s awaiting assistance, not- rather than repeatedly alerting the teacher.

transcript.speaker: Elena Ruiz
transcript.text: That works, as long as the waiting state stays quiet and doesn't become one more thing the teacher has to explain to a child. I do want us to be explicit in the packet that a delayed reseat may mean an, um, unusable recording, but it's not a reason to exclude that student or make the class redo the session. Maya, is that consistent with the eight-clean-minute threshold?

transcript.speaker: Arun Patel
transcript.text: Yeah, that seems reasonable.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: The eight clean minutes is an analytic inclusion threshold, not a target staff have to achieve. If delayed reseating leaves us with less than that, we keep the session and its quality metadata, but exclude it from the EEG feature estimate. Then once the district records start coming in March under the district-generated study IDs, we can model whether the missingness is patterned, rather than just dropping those children.

transcript.speaker: Elena Ruiz
transcript.text: And I want that missingness review to be part of the equity check, not just a technical appendix. If smaller students or students who move more are disproportionately below eight minutes, we need to say that plainly. The district outcomes can still be linked for everyone who consents, and we should not let usable EEG quietly become the definition of participation.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Beginning in March, when the de-identified attendance, reading, and referral files start arriving under the district study IDs, we should check linkage completeness alongside EEG missingness. Otherwise, we could end up calling a brain–behavior pattern when it’s really just differential data availability—

transcript.speaker: Elena Ruiz
transcript.text: Agreed. For the school packet, I think we should make that distinction really plain. Every consenting student stays in the pilot and in the district-record linkage, while a session may or may not yield an EEG estimate. I still need to check the consent and assent language against Riverview's family-accessibility requirements, but I don't want families hearing "data quality" as though their child has failed the- failed participation.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Yes—that wording keeps participation separate from signal yield, which is important.

transcript.speaker: Elena Ruiz
transcript.text: Participation isn't contingent on producing a usable signal. That's the language we should use with families and teachers. Before we close, I just want to confirm the district extract is still the sole outcome source. Attendance, reading assessment, and referrals, so teachers aren't being asked to keep separate outcome logs.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: From my side, those three district extracts are enough as the outcome sources, assuming the reading file includes the assessment date and instrument so we can account for spring timing and any across-room differences. And in the packet, I’d call any EEG–outcome result an association. I lost my thread there, but it’s not evidence by itself that the neurofeedback improved learning.

transcript.speaker: Elena Ruiz
transcript.text: And I’d add that the reading measure isn’t interchangeable across instruments, so the extract needs the instrument and the date, like Maya said, not just a score. I’m comfortable keeping the claims modest for this pilot, feasibility, signal yield, and associations with the district outcomes, not saying we’ve demonstrated improved learning, and—

transcript.speaker: Arun Patel
transcript.text: On the engineering side, I can support that framing. We’ll have session delivery, device assignment, and signal-quality records after encrypted upload. I’m still verifying the final label inventory before I commit to the exact classroom allocation. Two units are in the post-usability firmware check. And one small thing, I saw two odd battery drops without a matching usage error, so I’d rather resolve- I want to know whether that’s the dock or the reporting before we put a device list in the packet.

transcript.speaker: Elena Ruiz
transcript.text: Don’t put a fixed device-to-classroom list in the school packet until those checks are resolved. We can- instead, we can describe the equipment and the non-blocking staff procedure without promising an allocation that may change. I’ll review the consent and assent language against the district accessibility standards, and then we should be ready to submit with the outcome claims kept at feasibility and association.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Okay, I think we should leave it there—I’ll follow up by email on the analytic language once the packet is, is circulating. Thanks, everyone.

transcript.speaker: Elena Ruiz
transcript.text: Thank you. Goodbye, everyone.

transcript.speaker: Arun Patel
transcript.text: All right, take care.

transcript.speaker: Arun Patel
transcript.text: Hi, everyone. I've got the revised child-size bands and the charging cart ready to go. So I was hoping we could, today, pressure-test the classroom setup a bit. Where the cart actually lives, the end-of-day routine, and any last concerns before we hand things over to schools.

transcript.speaker: Elena Ruiz
transcript.text: Sorry, I'm a couple of minutes late. Where have you got to? Arun, on the cart and the end-of-day routine, I'd want the classroom-facing version to be very spare. Teachers should know where it lives and where used bands go, but they shouldn't be responsible for checking charge or resolving contact problems during instruction.

transcript.speaker: Arun Patel
transcript.text: Yeah, that's important.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: And from my side, the aide-facing step really should stay to one reseat, then mark the contact as not restored and move on. Arun, after that reseat, what exactly does the revised contact flag do? Does it reset the quality state in a way we can distinguish downstream? I'm asking because of those two broad drops in the usability recordings. I need timestamps and the raw, raw quality label even when the session is poor.

transcript.speaker: Arun Patel
transcript.text: It does. The reseat creates a timestamped event, and the device keeps writing the raw contact-quality stream. It doesn't overwrite the earlier state or make a poor segment look clean. I'll make sure the export includes the flag transitions and the aide's not-restored mark, so you can line those broad drops up with what actually happened.

transcript.speaker: Elena Ruiz
transcript.text: Good, that gives us a clean record without asking the teacher to interpret it. Maya, could you say a little more about ordinary writing posture, looking down and shifting over a worksheet? One teacher pointed out that a calm reading block can still involve quite a bit of movement when the work is difficult, and I don't want staff treating that as disruption or as a child, a child doing something wrong.

transcript.speaker: Arun Patel
transcript.text: Mm, right.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Ordinary down-gaze and small posture shifts can make a dry frontal contact look worse, even when the child is completely on task. I’d keep the activity code descriptive, reading, writing, head down, maybe adjustment if it’s observed. I wouldn’t- I wouldn’t treat a quality drop as a behavioral event. Elena, do teachers have cues they use when a child starts fiddling with something they’re wearing? That may be more informative than trying to infer it from the EEG.

transcript.speaker: Elena Ruiz
transcript.text: They do, although it's pretty ordinary classroom judgment. It's repeated touching, taking it off, or turning around to get a peer's attention, not just one quick adjustment. I’d be careful not to ask teachers to make that another coded judgment, though. Could the aide just select an observed “fiddling/removal” code when it’s clear, and otherwise leave the activity description alone?
